stories.title: Bangkok night markets: choose the right evening
stories.dek: Five options for food, vintage browsing or a riverside outing, with a simple way to plan your evening.
body: Pick the market that fits your evening rather than trying to visit all five. One main destination, a meal and time to browse will usually make a more relaxed plan than crossing the city between several stops.
The market locations and transport references below come from a guide updated in August 2026. They are a research starting point, not a live confirmation that every stall is trading tonight.

sections.h: An evening that leaves room to explore
p: Start by checking the location, listed opening day and weather. On arrival, take one short lap before ordering; seeing the menus first makes it easier to compare dishes and avoid spending your whole food budget at the first stall.

Choose a main dish, then decide whether you want a snack or dessert. Keep your shopping allowance separate. If you are tired after dinner, finish there: a second market is an option, not a requirement.

sections.h: Plan the journey home before dinner
p: Check the relevant rail operator’s last-train information for your route, including any connection. A market’s closing time is not the same as the last train back to your accommodation.
If you plan to return by taxi or ride-hailing service, check the price and pickup point before committing. Keep money for that journey separate from shopping.

sections.h: If the weather or crowds change the plan
p: Use the current forecast and conditions at the market to decide whether to continue. A covered stall does not make every walkway sheltered. Keep a nearby indoor meal or an earlier return as your fallback.
If your main goal is conversation or an unhurried meal, you can change the plan instead of queuing at a popular stall. Ask about the wait before ordering.

tips: Bring smaller banknotes and check payment options at each stall.
Check the price before ordering seafood or dishes sold by weight.
Confirm opening days; the five destinations do not share one schedule.
faq: Can I combine the two Ratchada markets?
The source lists them near the same MRT station. Choose one first and add the other only if time, weather and energy allow.
Is everything included in free admission?
No. Food, shopping, rides and other attractions are separate purchases.
Will all stalls open in rain?
Do not assume so. Check the operator’s latest notices and have an alternative plan.
quickPlan: Best for
An evening of eating and browsing; choose by location and interests.
Time to allow
Our suggestion: 2–3 hours at one market, plus travel.
Budget approach
Separate food, shopping and the journey home. Set a spending limit before browsing; admission does not cover purchases or attractions.

stories.title: Bangkok's big temples in one day
stories.dek: A practical route through the Grand Palace, Wat Pho and Wat Arun, with admission costs, a shorter option and time for lunch.
body: Three major landmarks in one day can be rewarding, but the aim is to enjoy them rather than finish a checklist. Start with the Grand Palace, walk south to Wat Pho, then cross the river for Wat Arun. Keep Wat Saket as an optional extra, not a fourth compulsory stop.
This is a suggested itinerary based on published visitor information, not a route we claim to have tested in person. Allow space for queues, heat and a proper lunch break.

items.text: The first stop. Its ticket includes Wat Phra Kaew and the Queen Sirikit Museum of Textiles.
The second stop. Leave a separate slot if you want to enquire about a massage.
The third stop, across the river. You can appreciate the architecture without climbing every step.
Optional: save this for another outing if the first three stops have filled your day.

sections.h: If you only have half a day
p: Our recommendation is to choose two sites rather than hurry through all three. Grand Palace plus Wat Pho keeps you on the same bank; Wat Pho plus Wat Arun makes a shorter route with a river crossing. Choose the royal complex if that is your priority, or leave it for another day if you prefer a slower visit.

sections.h: Build the budget before you go
p: The ฿1,000 admission total is the sum of the three published foreign-adult fees, not a combined ticket. Each site controls its own admission. Different eligibility rules may apply to children and Thai visitors.

Add your hotel-to-route transport, lunch, drinking water, ferry fare and any optional service separately. Check menus and fare boards before paying. The Grand Palace’s official pages show ticket sales ending at 3:30pm but give differing closing-hour information, so consult its dated schedule instead of planning a late arrival.

sections.h: Dress for entry and for walking
p: Choose a sleeved top and loose clothing covering the knees; the Grand Palace also lists restrictions on tight, torn and transparent clothing. Wear shoes you can remove when required. Follow each chapel’s photography notices and leave space for worshippers.

For visitors using a wheelchair, travelling with a stroller or avoiding steps, check the sites’ accessibility information and the ferry boarding arrangements in advance. A close cluster of landmarks does not mean every transfer is step-free.

Use the map links below to check the walk between the Grand Palace and Wat Pho. For Wat Arun, ask at the riverside pier for the current cross-river service and fare. Pier access and service arrangements can change.
If a stranger says a site is closed, verify it through the official schedule or staff at the entrance before accepting an alternative tour. Avoid building the day around an unconfirmed last boat.
The linked cultural guide provides additional background on these Bangkok landmarks. Use it for context alongside the official visitor information linked above.

tips: Carry water, sun protection and a small amount of cash.
Check the Grand Palace’s dated schedule before leaving your hotel.
Leave the optional fourth stop out if the day feels rushed.
faq: Is there a combined ticket for all three?
No combined ticket is assumed in this itinerary. The budget adds the separate published admission fees.
Do I need to book a guide?
A guide is optional. If you arrange one, check what is included and agree the fee before starting.
Can I add a massage at Wat Pho?
Ask the school about availability and charges. Budget extra time rather than fitting it inside the one-hour temple visit.
quickPlan: Best for
First-time visitors interested in temples and architecture.
Time to allow
Our planning allowance: 5–6 hours with lunch; longer if you add Wat Saket.
Admission budget

stories.title: Nine Bangkok street food names worth knowing
stories.dek: Choose a neighbourhood, match it to your appetite and plan a few food stops instead of racing around all nine.
body: Nine names give you options, not a nine-stop challenge. Choose two or three that are close enough for the time you have, and leave room to change your mind when you see the menu or the queue.
This is a research-based shortlist, not a set of first-hand taste reviews. Prices in older listings are useful context but should not replace the menu displayed when you visit.

items.text: Start here for pad thai.
Make this a deliberate choice for the dish, price and queue, rather than an automatic stop.
Order the oyster omelette crisp.
For peppery rolled noodles on Yaowarat Road.
Start with a small order and add more if you want it.

sections.h: Order one thing you can identify
p: If there is no English menu, a photograph or a displayed dish can help you explain what you want. Ask the price and portion size before ordering, especially for seafood. Start with one dish and order more after you see the serving.

Condiments and ordering conventions differ between shops. Taste before adding chilli or sauce, and ask staff if you are unsure. Pointing can help with a dish; it is not a dependable way to communicate an allergy.

sections.h: Make dietary requirements part of the choice
p: A dish without visible meat may still contain fish sauce, oyster sauce, shrimp paste or a meat-based stock. Ask about the ingredients and preparation, using a written Thai translation where helpful. If the vendor cannot confirm what you need, choose another option.

No busy stall, familiar dish or type of ice can guarantee food safety. Choose food and drinks you are comfortable with, and avoid relying on a general travel guide for assurances about a specific kitchen.

sections.h: Treat the famous stop as an optional splurge
p: The MICHELIN listing for Jay Fai identifies cash-only payment and warns visitors to expect a queue. Check that listing and the restaurant’s current arrangements before setting aside time for a visit.

Our planning advice is to decide how much time and money you want to spend before joining a queue. Keep another meal option in mind; enjoying Bangkok food does not require eating at its most famous address.
Use the map links to check the distance between your chosen stops. Do not group places simply because they appear next to each other in a list.
If a shop is closed or has sold out, move to your backup rather than let one missing dish dictate the day. Finish with a drink or dessert only if you still want one.

tips: Carry cash, but check the shop’s accepted payment methods.
Read the displayed menu before using an old quoted price.
Ask before photographing staff or a working kitchen.
faq: Can I visit all nine in a day?
The list is intended as a selection. Choose a small cluster and save the other neighbourhoods for another outing.
Can I find vegetarian options?
Possibly, but ingredients need checking. A vegetarian sign or a meat-free appearance is not a substitute for explaining your requirements.
Do I need to queue at Jay Fai?
It depends on the restaurant’s current arrangements. Check before travelling and have another food option if the wait exceeds your plan.
quickPlan: Best for
Visitors who want a manageable introduction to Bangkok food.
Time to allow
Our suggestion: one neighbourhood and 2–3 stops over 2–3 hours.
Budget approach
Check a main dish, drink and optional dessert on the menu. Famous seafood specialists can cost much more than a simple noodle or rice meal.

stories.title: Bangkok from above: four rooftops
stories.dek: Where to go for the view, and how high each one actually is.
body: Rooftop bars are one of the things Bangkok does better than almost anywhere. Drinks cost several times what they do at street level, and most venues ask for closed shoes and long trousers for men. Arrive before sunset for a seat at the rail.

items.text: The highest. Ticketed, with a glass floor.
The famous one, 63 floors up.
Open to the sky on the 61st floor.
More relaxed, with a full circle of view.

sections.h: Why Bangkok does this so well
p: The city is flat, dense and warm after dark all year, so a bar on a roof needs no heating and has nothing to block the view. Hotels started opening their rooftops to drinkers in the early 2000s and the idea spread quickly.

sections.h: Dress codes and what it costs
p: The big hotel bars ask for smart casual clothes. For men that usually means long trousers and closed shoes. Sleeveless shirts, sportswear and flip-flops are turned away at the lift.

Menus normally show prices before a 10 per cent service charge and 7 per cent tax, so the bill is about 17 per cent higher than the list price. Expect to pay several times what the same drink costs at street level. You are paying for the view.

Sunset in Bangkok falls between about 6pm and 6.45pm depending on the time of year. Arrive 45 minutes before for a seat at the rail and stay as the city lights come on. In the rainy season, open-air decks close at short notice when storms pass through, so have a second plan.

King Power Mahanakhon, designed by the architect Ole Scheeren, was the tallest building in Thailand when it was completed in 2016 and remains one of the two tallest. Its pixelated outline, as though a ribbon of blocks had been removed, makes it easy to pick out from anywhere in the city. The SkyWalk is a ticketed observation deck rather than a bar, though there is a bar at the top.

tips: Some venues require a booking for rail-side tables at sunset.
Tripods and professional cameras are often not allowed.
If heights bother you, skip the glass floor at Mahanakhon and stay on the main deck.
For a cheaper view, the Golden Mount in the old town looks over the low-rise city at sunset.
faq: Is there a minimum age?
The legal drinking age in Thailand is 20, and hotel bars check identification. Some rooftops do not admit children in the evening at all, so check before bringing a family.
Do I need a reservation?
For a table at the rail around sunset, yes, at the best-known bars. Standing room at the bar is usually available without one.
Can I go up just for the view?
Bars expect you to order at least one drink, and a few set a minimum spend. If you only want the view, the Mahanakhon SkyWalk is a ticketed observation deck with no need to buy anything else.
What happens if it rains?
Open-air sections close during storms and staff move guests under cover. Storms usually pass within an hour, and the air afterwards is clearer for photographs.

stories.title: How to do Chatuchak without getting lost
stories.dek: More than 15,000 stalls, open at weekends only. A plan helps.
body: Chatuchak Weekend Market opens on Saturdays and Sundays from 9am to 6pm, with a smaller Friday evening session. On weekdays most stalls are shut.

Arrive by 10am. Take the BTS to Mo Chit or the MRT to Chatuchak Park or Kamphaeng Phet. The market is divided into numbered sections: clothes, ceramics, plants, antiques and food each have their own area.
By midday the lanes are hot. Break for lunch across the road at Or Tor Kor Market, where the curry stalls are open daily until 8pm, then go back for a second pass.

p: Bangkok's weekend market used to be held at Sanam Luang, the royal field beside the Grand Palace. In 1982 it moved north to its present site beside Chatuchak Park. Locals call it JJ, from the Thai spelling of its name.

The market is laid out as a ring. A main walkway loops around the edge and numbered lanes run off it into 27 sections. The clock tower near the centre is the standard meeting point if your group gets separated, which it will.

Pick two or three sections that interest you and go to those first. Vintage clothing, ceramics and home decoration are the strongest. If you see something you want, buy it. Finding the same stall again an hour later is harder than it sounds.

sections.h: What to buy and how to bargain
p: Good buys include hand-painted ceramics, woven baskets, linen clothing from young Thai designers and second-hand denim. Many stalls now have fixed prices. Where they do not, ask for a small discount with a smile, and expect a better price for two or three items than for one.

Food stalls are scattered through every section. Coconut ice cream, grilled pork skewers and Thai iced tea are the classics. When the heat gets too much, JJ Mall next door is air-conditioned, and Or Tor Kor Market across the road has a calmer food court.

tips: Take the MRT to Kamphaeng Phet for the quickest way in. Exit 2 opens straight into the market.
Bring cash. There are ATMs, but the queues are long by midday.
Several stalls near the main gates will pack and ship large purchases home for you.
Wear closed, comfortable shoes. The lanes are uneven and wet in places.
faq: Is Chatuchak open on weekdays?

The main market is a weekend event. A smaller Friday evening session runs for early shoppers. On other days most of the lanes are shuttered, although the surrounding malls and Or Tor Kor Market are open.
How long should I allow?
Three to four hours is enough for most people. Collectors and serious shoppers can easily spend the whole day.
Is there anywhere to cool down?
Most of the market is covered but not air-conditioned. JJ Mall and Mixt Chatuchak, two shopping centres on the edge of the market, are air-conditioned and have food courts and clean toilets.
Can I pay by card?
Rarely. Bring cash. Some stalls accept Thai QR payments, which most foreign banking apps cannot use.

stories.title: Loy Krathong 2026 falls on 24 to 25 November
stories.dek: Where to float a krathong in Bangkok, and why the published dates differ by a day.
body: Loy Krathong takes place on the full-moon night of the twelfth Thai lunar month. This year sources give either 24 or 25 November, so check the programme of the venue you plan to visit.
In Bangkok the main gatherings are along the Chao Phraya: at Wat Arun, at Wat Yannawa and at Asiatique The Riverfront.
A krathong is a small float made of banana trunk and leaves with a candle, incense and flowers. Choose one made from natural materials rather than foam.

p: Loy means to float and a krathong is the small decorated raft. By setting one on the water, people give thanks to the goddess of water and symbolically let go of bad luck and resentment from the past year. Many make a wish as the candle drifts away.

The custom is often traced to the old kingdom of Sukhothai and to a court lady named Nang Noppamas, who is said to have made the first lotus-shaped krathong. Historians treat the story as legend, but it is the one every Thai child learns at school.
The riverside temples and Asiatique draw the biggest crowds. City parks with lakes usually stay open late for the evening and are calmer, especially for families.
Piers and river boats are very busy from late afternoon. If you want to be by the Chao Phraya, arrive before sunset and plan to stay in one place.

Traditional krathongs are made from a slice of banana trunk wrapped in folded banana leaves and topped with flowers, a candle and incense. Some vendors sell versions made of bread that fish can eat. Avoid foam bases and plastic decorations. City workers collect several hundred thousand krathongs from the water the next morning, and natural ones are far easier to deal with.

tips: Releasing sky lanterns or setting off fireworks without permission is illegal in Bangkok.
You can buy a krathong at any temple gate or pier on the night.
Dress modestly if you plan to go into a temple.
Expect road closures near the river and allow extra time to get home.
faq: Can visitors take part?
Yes, and you will be welcomed. Buy a krathong, light the candle and incense, make a wish and set it on the water. Some people add a coin or a strand of hair.
What time should I go?
Celebrations begin at dusk and are busiest between about 7pm and 10pm. Arrive before sunset if you want a place at the water's edge.
Where do I buy a krathong?
Vendors sell them at every temple gate, pier and park entrance on the night. They are inexpensive. Many schools and community groups also sell handmade ones to raise funds.
Is it safe by the river?
The piers and floating pontoons become very crowded. Keep hold of children, do not push onto a platform that is already full, and consider a park lake instead if you are with a family.

stories.title: Bangkok Art Biennale opens on 29 October
stories.dek: Four months of contemporary art in temples, galleries and riverside venues.
body: The Bangkok Art Biennale runs from 29 October 2026 to 28 February 2027. Works are shown across the city, including inside working temples, which makes it a good reason to revisit the old town.
Temple venues keep their usual dress code and entry fees.

p: The Bangkok Art Biennale was first held in 2018 and has returned every two years since. It brings Thai and international artists together and places their work in public buildings, shopping centres and working temples as well as galleries.
Past editions have shown work at Wat Pho, Wat Arun and the Bangkok Art and Culture Centre. Seeing contemporary sculpture in a temple courtyard is the part most visitors remember.

Venues are spread across the city, so group them. The old-town temple venues fit into one day on foot and by ferry. The central venues around Pathum Wan fit into another and are linked by the BTS Skytrain.
Entry to the Bangkok Art and Culture Centre is free. Temples charge their normal admission and keep their usual dress code.

tips: Pick up the printed venue map at the first site you visit.
Weekday mornings are quietest.
Temple venues close earlier than galleries, so do those first.
faq: Is the Biennale free?
Many venues are, including the Bangkok Art and Culture Centre. Temples that host works charge their usual admission.
How much time do I need?
Two days covers the main clusters comfortably: one for the old-town and riverside venues, one for the central galleries. With a single day, pick one area and do it properly.
Is it suitable for children?
The large, colourful installations in the galleries tend to delight children. Temple venues ask for quiet and modest dress, which suits older children better.
Can I take photographs?
Usually, without flash, unless a sign beside the work says otherwise. Inside temple chapels, follow the temple's own rules.
When is the best time to go?
The exhibition overlaps Bangkok's cool season. From November to February the weather is at its best for walking between venues.

stories.title: Big shows in Bangkok before the year ends
stories.dek: The Weeknd, Baby Monster, My Chemical Romance and BTS are all on the calendar.
body: The last quarter of 2026 is a heavy one for stadium shows. The Weeknd plays Rajamangala National Stadium from 11 to 13 October. Jason Mraz is at BITEC Bangna on 29 October.
November brings Baby Monster to Impact Arena on the 7th and 8th and My Chemical Romance to Impact Challenger Hall on the 17th. BTS play Rajamangala on 3, 5 and 6 December.
Out of town, Wonderfruit returns to The Fields at Siam Country Club near Pattaya from 3 to 7 December.

p: Rajamangala National Stadium, in the Hua Mak district east of the centre, was built for the 1998 Asian Games and holds roughly 50,000 people. It is where the biggest international tours play.

Impact Arena and Impact Challenger Hall are part of a large exhibition complex at Muang Thong Thani, north of the city in Nonthaburi province. BITEC is in Bang Na, in the south-east, with a BTS station at its door. UOB Live, a newer hall inside the EmSphere mall on Sukhumvit Road, opened in 2024.

No train stops at the stadium gate. Most people ride the Airport Rail Link to Ramkhamhaeng station and continue by taxi, motorcycle taxi or bus. After a show, tens of thousands of people leave at once, and taxis are scarce for an hour or more. Walking ten to fifteen minutes away from the stadium before calling a car usually works better than waiting at the gate.

Muang Thong Thani used to be reachable only by road. A branch of the Pink Line monorail now runs into the complex, which makes the trip from the city much more predictable. Leave early anyway. Security checks and merchandise queues are long on show nights.

tips: Buy tickets only from the promoter's official seller. Resale at inflated prices is common for big tours.
Open-air stadium shows go ahead in rain. Bring a poncho, since umbrellas are usually banned.
Large bags and professional cameras are generally not allowed inside.
Agree a meeting point with friends before the show. Mobile data slows to a crawl in the crowd.
faq: How early should I arrive?
For a stadium show, two to three hours before the start. Security checks, ticket scanning and merchandise queues all take longer than you expect.
Are the shows seated or standing?
Stadium concerts usually have standing zones on the pitch and numbered seats in the stands. Your ticket will name a zone. Arena shows vary by tour.
What can I bring in?
Rules are set by each promoter and are published before the show. Small bags are normally fine. Large backpacks, umbrellas, professional cameras and outside drinks are commonly refused.
How do I get home afterwards?
The BTS and MRT stop running around midnight. If the show ends late, arrange a ride in advance or be prepared to walk away from the venue before finding a taxi.

stories.title: A slow afternoon in Talat Noi
stories.dek: Engine parts, shrine smoke and coffee by the river. Give this old neighbourhood four hours.
body: Talat Noi is where Bangkok keeps its spare parts. Whole lanes are stacked with gearboxes and drive shafts, pulled from old cars and sold by families who have worked the same doorway for generations.

Start at the river and walk inland without a plan. The lanes are too narrow for cars, so you move at the speed of the neighbourhood: past Chinese shrines with coils of incense overhead, the old So Heng Tai mansion, and walls that street artists have been filling in for years.
By four the light turns gold on the river side. Find a cafe with a terrace and watch the express boats fight the current. Dinner in Chinatown is a fifteen-minute walk north.

p: Talat Noi means little market. It is one of Bangkok's oldest riverside communities, settled by Chinese traders and by Portuguese Catholics who moved here after the fall of Ayutthaya. The Holy Rosary Church, which locals call Kalawar, was founded by the Portuguese community in the 1780s. The present cream-coloured building dates from the 1890s.

The So Heng Tai mansion, a courtyard house in the southern Chinese style, is more than two centuries old and is still owned by descendants of the family who built it. Today the courtyard holds a deep pool used by a diving school.

From Hua Lamphong MRT station it is a ten-minute walk to Soi Wanit 2, the lane that runs the length of the neighbourhood. Follow it past the engine-part shops, look in at the small Chinese shrines and turn towards the river whenever a side lane opens up.
The rusted shell of an old Fiat, parked against a wall for decades, has become the most photographed object in the area. Street art is concentrated in the lanes near it.
Families live and work in these lanes. Keep your voice down, do not photograph people at work without asking, and step aside for the motorbikes and handcarts that have right of way.

tips: Go on a weekday afternoon. Workshops are open and the lanes are quieter than at weekends.
Many cafes close by 6pm.
River City, a short walk south, has clean toilets and air conditioning.
The Chao Phraya Express Boat stops nearby if you would rather leave by river.
faq: How long should I spend there?
Two hours is enough to walk the main lanes. Allow four if you want to sit in a cafe, visit the shrines and take photographs.
Can I go inside the So Heng Tai mansion?
It is a private family home. Visitors are generally welcome in the courtyard when the gate is open, and are expected to buy a drink from the small cafe there.
How do I get there?
Walk ten minutes from Hua Lamphong MRT station, or arrive by river boat. Taxis struggle in the narrow lanes, so ask to be dropped on Charoen Krung Road.
Where should I eat?
There are cafes in the neighbourhood itself. For a full meal, Chinatown's Yaowarat Road is fifteen minutes north on foot and comes alive after dark.

stories.title: Day trips from Bangkok you can do by train
stories.dek: An ancient capital, a market on the tracks and a beach, all without a car.
body: Ayutthaya is the easy one. The capital of Siam from 1351 to 1767, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is under two hours north by train. Hire a bicycle outside the station.
For something stranger, head south-west to Samut Songkhram, where stallholders at the Maeklong Railway Market pull back their awnings each time a train rolls through.
Beach people should start early for Hua Hin. It is a long day, but the old wooden station, with its royal waiting room, is one of the prettiest in the country.

p: Ayutthaya was one of the largest cities in the world in the 1600s, a trading capital on an island ringed by three rivers. A Burmese army sacked it in 1767 and the court never returned. What remains is a park of brick towers and headless Buddha statues spread among modern streets.

Three sites make a satisfying day. Wat Mahathat has the stone Buddha head held in the roots of a fig tree. Wat Phra Si Sanphet has three bell-shaped chedis in a row, the image on most postcards. Wat Chaiwatthanaram, on the river to the west, is at its best in late afternoon light.
From the station, a small ferry crosses the river to the island for a few baht. Bicycle and scooter rental shops line the lane on the far side.

The Maeklong Railway Market in Samut Songkhram is nicknamed the umbrella-pulling market. Vendors lay their produce right up to the rails and fold back their awnings when the train's horn sounds. The train passes only a few times a day, so check the timetable before you set out.
Getting there by rail is an adventure in itself: two short local lines with a river ferry between them. The Amphawa floating market is nearby and operates on weekend afternoons.

Hua Hin became a royal seaside resort in the 1920s and still has a quieter, more old-fashioned feel than the island beaches. A new elevated station opened in 2023 beside the original red-and-cream wooden building, which has been kept. The beach is a ten-minute walk from the platform.

tips: Most long-distance trains now leave from Krung Thep Aphiwat Central Terminal, not the old Hua Lamphong station. Check your ticket.
Third-class tickets are very cheap and are sold at the station on the day.
Take the earliest train out and a mid-afternoon train back to avoid travelling in the dark.
Carry water. Ayutthaya has little shade.
faq: Can I visit Ayutthaya without a guide?
Easily. Rent a bicycle or hire a tuk-tuk with a driver for a few hours outside the station. The main ruins are signposted in English.
Is there an entrance fee at Ayutthaya?
The major temples each charge a small fee for foreign visitors, and a combined pass covering several of them is usually sold at the ticket booths.
Is the train better than a minivan?
The train is slower, cheaper and more interesting, and it avoids Bangkok's traffic. Minivans are quicker door to door but less comfortable.
What is the best time of year?
November to February, when it is cooler and dry. In any season, do the ruins early and late and spend the middle of the day over lunch.

stories.title: Four Bangkok hotels with a story
stories.dek: A grand dame from 1876, a riverside tower and the hotel that topped a world ranking.
body: Bangkok's best-known hotels line the Chao Phraya. Staying on the river means slower travel and better evenings. These four are worth knowing even if you only visit for tea or a drink.

items.text: The classic.
Across the water, with river views from every room.
Small, private and a boat ride from the sights.
The newest of the four.

p: Where you sleep shapes the trip more than the hotel does. The river is slower and more scenic, with boats as your main transport. Sukhumvit Road is modern, crowded and convenient, with the BTS Skytrain overhead and restaurants open late. The old town puts you within walking distance of the temples but far from any train.
First-time visitors with three or four days often split the stay: two nights by the river for the sights, then two on Sukhumvit for food and shopping.

You do not need a room key to enjoy the grand hotels. Afternoon tea in the Authors' Lounge at the Mandarin Oriental is a Bangkok tradition, and most riverside hotels welcome outside guests in their bars and restaurants. Hotel shuttle boats run from the pier beside Saphan Taksin BTS station and are free to use if you are heading to the hotel.

High season runs from November to February, when the weather is driest and coolest. Rates are at their highest then, and around Christmas and New Year in particular. Prices drop noticeably in the rainy months from June to October, when you can often get a river-view room for the price of a standard one.

tips: Check whether the rate includes the 10 per cent service charge and 7 per cent tax.
Riverside hotels look close together on a map but can be a long taxi ride apart. Use the boats.
Ask for a high floor on the river side. Lower rooms can be noisy from boat traffic.
Smart dress is expected in hotel restaurants in the evening.
faq: How many nights do I need in Bangkok?
Three or four nights is a good first visit. That gives a day for the temples, a day for markets and neighbourhoods, and time for a day trip or simply for eating.
Which area is best for first-timers?
The riverside if sightseeing is your priority, or Sukhumvit near a BTS station if you want restaurants and nightlife on your doorstep.
How do I get from the airport?
From Suvarnabhumi, the Airport Rail Link runs to the city in under half an hour and connects with the BTS and MRT. Metered taxis add an airport surcharge and motorway tolls to the fare.
Should I tip at hotels?
A service charge is already added to hotel bills. Small tips for porters and housekeeping are appreciated but not required.

stories.title: Yi Peng 2026: the lantern rules, and where to watch
stories.dek: The festival is on 24 and 25 November. Releasing a sky lantern in the city can land you in court.
body: Yi Peng, the northern lantern festival, coincides with Loy Krathong on 24 and 25 November 2026. The free celebrations are in the old city: Tha Phae Gate, the Three Kings Monument, Wat Phan Tao and Wat Chedi Luang, which fill with candles and paper lanterns.
Krathongs are floated on the Ping River near Nawarat Bridge and on the old city moat.

Sky lanterns are tightly controlled because of fire and air-traffic risk. Unlicensed releases are banned across Mueang Chiang Mai district and neighbouring areas, with penalties of up to five years in prison and a fine of up to ฿200,000. The mass releases you see in photographs happen at licensed, ticketed venues outside the city.

p: Yi Peng is a festival of the old Lanna kingdom of northern Thailand. In the Lanna calendar, yi means two and peng means full moon, so the name simply marks the full moon of the second month. It falls at the same time as Loy Krathong, which is celebrated across the whole country, and in Chiang Mai the two have merged into several days of light.

Lanterns come in more than one kind. Houses, shops and temples hang paper lanterns from their eaves and gates. The famous floating ones, called khom loi, are cylinders of thin paper with a fuel cell at the base, released as an act of making merit and letting go of misfortune.

The photographs of thousands of lanterns rising together are taken at organised events outside the city. These are ticketed, often expensive and usually sell out months ahead. Tickets normally include transport from town, dinner and lanterns.
Buy from the organiser or a licensed agent, and be cautious of resellers on social media. If an offer appears in the last week at a bargain price, treat it with suspicion.

You do not need a ticket to enjoy the festival. On both evenings the old city fills with candles set along temple walls and the moat. Monks hold chanting ceremonies at several temples, and a parade of illuminated floats usually passes along Tha Phae Road.
Down at the river, families launch krathongs from the banks near Nawarat Bridge. It is crowded, smoky from fireworks and thoroughly good-natured.

Because of the lanterns, Chiang Mai airport adjusts its schedule on festival nights and some evening flights are moved or cancelled. If you are flying in or out, check with your airline a few days before. Hotels in and around the old city fill early, so book well ahead.

tips: Do not release a sky lantern in town. The penalties are severe and are enforced.
Wear clothes you do not mind getting marked by candle wax or ash.
Carry cash for krathongs and street food. ATMs near the river run dry on the night.
Agree a meeting point. Mobile networks slow down in the crowds around Tha Phae Gate.
faq: Can I release a sky lantern myself?
Not inside the city. Releases are banned across central Chiang Mai and nearby districts and are allowed only at licensed venues. The penalties include prison and a heavy fine.
Is Yi Peng the same as Loy Krathong?
They are two festivals held at the same time. Yi Peng is the northern tradition of lanterns. Loy Krathong, celebrated across Thailand, is about floating small rafts on water.
How far ahead should I book?
Several months for a room in or near the old city, and as early as tickets go on sale for the organised lantern releases.
Are the lanterns bad for the environment?
They cause litter and are a fire and aviation hazard, which is why the rules are strict. If you attend a paid release, choose an organiser that collects the fallen lanterns afterwards.

stories.title: Chiang Mai's markets, day by day
stories.dek: Friday morning, Saturday night, Sunday night, and three that open every day.
body: Chiang Mai keeps a market calendar. Plan a weekend around it and you will eat well and carry home more than you meant to.

items.text: Friday, early. Go for breakfast.
Saturday evening.
Sunday evening, and the one not to miss.
Any day, for food to take home.
Any evening, for a cheap dinner.
Any night, if you still need souvenirs.

p: The walking streets are closed to traffic and laid out as one long lane with stalls on both sides and down the middle. Go with the flow of people on the way out and come back on the other side. Almost everything is paid for in cash, so bring small notes.
Prices are fair to begin with and bargaining is gentle. Asking for a little off when you buy two or three things is fine. Haggling hard over a few baht is not the custom here.

Northern food is different from what you find in Bangkok. Look for sai ua, a coarse pork sausage scented with lemongrass and lime leaf, and for nam prik num, a roasted green-chilli dip eaten with crisp pork rinds and sticky rice. Rice noodles in a tomato and pork broth, called khanom jeen nam ngiao, are another regional dish.
At the Sunday market, several temples along the route open their courtyards as food courts with plastic tables. They are the best place to sit down.

Wualai Road has been the silversmiths' street for generations, and beaten silver bowls and jewellery are still made in workshops behind the shopfronts. Elsewhere, look for indigo-dyed cotton, embroidered textiles made by hill communities, celadon ceramics with their pale green glaze, and umbrellas and notebooks made from mulberry-bark paper.

The cool season from November to February is the most pleasant time for an evening outdoors. From about February to April, smoke from agricultural burning often causes heavy haze across the north. If you are visiting then, check the air quality and carry a mask.

tips: Arrive just after the stalls open for space to browse. By 7pm you will be shuffling.
When the national anthem plays at 6pm, stop and stand still like everyone else.
Public toilets are inside the temple grounds and ask for a small donation.
Red songthaews wait at both ends of each market for the ride home.
faq: Do the markets run in the rain?
In light rain, yes. A heavy storm will send many vendors home, particularly at the open-air walking streets.
Are they suitable for young children?
The Sunday market is extremely crowded by early evening. A baby carrier works better than a pushchair. Go as the stalls open at four for more space.
Can I send purchases home?
Yes. Post offices and courier shops in the city ship internationally, and some craft sellers will arrange shipping for larger pieces.
Where are the cash machines?
There are ATMs around Tha Phae Gate and along the moat road. Withdraw before you enter the market, as there are few inside.

stories.title: Where to start with khao soi
stories.dek: What makes a good bowl of the north's curry noodle, and where to order it.
body: Khao soi is egg noodles in a coconut curry broth, topped with a nest of the same noodles fried crisp. It comes with a side plate of pickled mustard greens, raw shallot and lime. Add all three, then taste before you reach for the chilli.
It is a daytime dish. Most specialist shops open in the morning and close by mid-afternoon.

items.text: The long-established name, across the river.
For the beef version.
Not khao soi, but the city's other must-order: braised pork leg.

p: Khao soi is thought to have arrived with Chin Haw traders, Muslim merchants from Yunnan who ran mule caravans between China, Burma and northern Thailand. That is why the oldest shops are halal and serve it with chicken or beef, never pork.

The name is probably related to the Burmese word for noodles, and the dish has a close cousin in Burma's coconut chicken noodle soup. The northern Thai version is richer in curry paste and always comes with the crown of fried noodles.

sections.h: What to look for in a bowl
p: The broth should be the colour of rust, with a film of red oil on top, and taste of dried chilli, turmeric and ginger before the coconut milk softens it. The noodles are flat, yellow and made with egg. The chicken is traditionally a whole drumstick, cooked until it falls apart.

The side plate is part of the dish. Pickled mustard greens add sourness, raw shallots add bite and a squeeze of lime lifts the whole bowl. A spoonful of chilli fried in oil is offered for those who want more heat.

sections.h: What else to order in the north
p: If khao soi wins you over, try the rest of the northern table. Kaeng hang le is a mild, slightly sweet pork curry with ginger and tamarind that shows Burmese influence. Nam prik ong is a dip of minced pork and tomato, served with raw vegetables. Sticky rice, eaten with the fingers, comes with everything.

tips: Go for an early lunch. The best-known shops close by mid-afternoon and sell out sooner.
A bowl is small by Western standards. Many people order two, or add a plate of satay.
Most khao soi shops take cash only.
Ask for mai phet if you want it mild. The chilli oil is always served on the side.
faq: Is khao soi spicy?
It is medium at most. The curry is rich and warming, and the fierce chilli oil is served separately for you to add.
Is there a vegetarian version?
Traditional shops make it with meat and often shrimp paste. Several vegetarian and vegan cafes in the old city offer versions with tofu or mushrooms.
Is it eaten for dinner?
Traditionally it is a lunch dish, and the specialist shops close in the afternoon. Tourist restaurants serve it all day.
Chicken or beef?
Chicken is the most common. Beef, slow-cooked until tender, is the choice at the older halal shops and is worth trying.

stories.title: Chiang Mai's old city on foot, gate to gate
stories.dek: A square mile of temples, lanes and cafes, wrapped in a moat.
body: The old city is a square, about a mile each side, with a moat around it. You can cross it in twenty-five minutes or lose a whole day inside.
Enter by Tha Phae Gate early, before the tour groups. Walk west along Ratchadamnoen Road to Wat Chedi Luang, whose ruined brick chedi dates from 1391, and on to Wat Phra Singh at the far end.
Most temples ask only that you cover your shoulders and take off your shoes. Leave the afternoon for the back lanes.

sections.h: Seven hundred years in a square
p: Chiang Mai means new city. King Mangrai founded it in 1296 as the capital of the Lanna kingdom, and the brick walls and moat were laid out as an almost perfect square. Much of the wall is gone, but the four corner bastions and five gates have been restored and the moat still holds water.

The gates are useful landmarks. Tha Phae faces east towards the river, Chang Phueak faces north, Suan Dok faces west and two gates open to the south. In the centre stands the Three Kings Monument, which shows Mangrai with the two allied rulers who helped him choose the site.
Wat Chiang Man, in the north-east corner, is the city's oldest temple, built by Mangrai when the city was founded. Its small chedi rests on a ring of stone elephants.

Wat Chedi Luang, in the middle of the old city, was once the tallest structure in Lanna. Its upper part collapsed in an earthquake in 1545 and has been left as a ruin, which makes it more impressive, not less. Some afternoons, monks sit at tables in the grounds for informal conversations with visitors who want to ask about Buddhism or monastic life.
Wat Phra Singh, at the western end of the main street, is the most important temple for local people and the most richly decorated.

The old city is flat and small enough to walk, though the midday heat makes a bicycle a good idea. Red pickup trucks with two benches in the back, called songthaews, work as shared taxis. Flag one down, tell the driver where you are going and pay a set fare for short hops when you get out.

sections.h: An old-city temple, then a separate excursion
p: The linked temple guide places Wat Chedi Luang inside the Old City and explains its importance to medieval Lanna history. Its brick stupa was damaged in the earthquake of 1545. The same guide describes Wat Umong’s meditation tunnels in the Suthep foothills, outside the walled centre.

Our planning suggestion: keep Chedi Luang within your walking day and treat Umong as a separate outing. This gives each place time without turning a short city walk into a cross-town checklist. Confirm visitor access and dress requirements directly with the temples.

tips: Start at 8am. The temples are quiet and the light is soft.
Carry a scarf or sarong to cover shoulders and knees.
Shoes come off at every chapel, so wear sandals.
Sunday is the best day to visit. The walking street market takes over the main road from late afternoon.
faq: How long do I need?
A full day lets you see three or four temples, stop for lunch and wander the lanes without hurrying.
Do the temples charge admission?
Most are free. A few of the largest ask foreign visitors for a small fee to enter the main hall.
Is it easy to cycle?
Yes. The ground is flat and the lanes inside the walls are quiet. Take care on the busy one-way roads that run along each side of the moat.
When is the best time of year?
November to February is cool and clear. March and April are hot and often hazy with smoke.

stories.title: Phuket Vegetarian Festival runs 10 to 18 October
stories.dek: Nine days of dawn processions, firecrackers and meat-free street food.
body: The Phuket Vegetarian Festival honours the Nine Emperor Gods of Taoist tradition. It opens with a pole-raising ceremony on the evening of 9 October and runs for nine days.

Devotees dress in white and keep a strict diet. Street processions leave the Chinese shrines early in the morning, with firecrackers loud enough to need earplugs. Some spirit mediums pierce their cheeks, which is not for everyone.
Look for yellow flags with red lettering. They mark stalls and restaurants serving the festival's meat-free food. Everything is free to watch.

p: According to local tradition, the festival dates from 1825. A travelling Chinese opera company performing for tin miners in Kathu, in the middle of the island, fell ill with a fever. The performers kept a strict vegetarian diet and prayed to the Nine Emperor Gods, and they recovered. The miners adopted the ritual and it has been held every year since.
It takes place during the first nine days of the ninth month of the Chinese lunar calendar, which is why the dates change each year.

Those taking part dress in white and follow a set of rules for the nine days. They eat no meat and drink no alcohol, and many also give up garlic, onions and other strong-smelling vegetables. The aim is to purify body and mind.

Food stalls that follow the rules fly yellow flags with red Chinese or Thai characters. Phuket Town is full of them, and the food is worth trying whether or not you are vegetarian: mock meats made from tofu and wheat, stir-fried noodles, fritters and sweets.

Each of the main Chinese shrines holds its own street procession on a different morning. Jui Tui and Bang Neow in Phuket Town and the shrine at Kathu are the largest. Spirit mediums walk in a trance, some with their cheeks pierced by skewers and other objects, while followers throw firecrackers at their feet.

There are also fire-walking and blade-ladder ceremonies in the shrine grounds on some evenings. On the last night, all the shrines carry their gods to the sea at Saphan Hin in a final procession that lasts past midnight.

tips: Bring earplugs and a face mask. The firecrackers are deafening and the smoke is thick.
Wear long sleeves and trousers in cotton. Sparks can melt synthetic fabric.
Processions start at dawn and close roads in Phuket Town until mid-morning.
The piercings are confronting. Stand back if you are squeamish, and never block a medium's path.
faq: Can anyone join in?
Yes. Everyone is welcome to watch the processions and eat at the vegetarian stalls. You do not need to follow the nine-day rules unless you choose to.
Do I have to wear white?
Only if you take part in a procession or enter the inner areas of a shrine. Spectators can wear ordinary modest clothing, though white is appreciated.
Is it suitable for children?
The food stalls and shrine fairs are fine for families. The street processions are extremely loud and include graphic piercings, so use your judgment.
Are normal restaurants open?
Yes. Most restaurants carry on as usual, and the beach resorts are hardly affected. The festival is concentrated in Phuket Town and Kathu.

stories.title: Phuket's Big Buddha is open again
stories.dek: The hilltop landmark reopened in March after 18 months closed.
body: The Big Buddha on Nakkerd Hill closed on 23 August 2024 after a landslide below the site killed 13 people. It reopened on 3 March 2026 and has stayed open since.
Visiting hours are 9am to 6pm, with last entry at 5.30pm. Entry is free. Shoulders and knees must be covered, and sarongs are lent at the entrance.

p: Work on the Big Buddha began in 2004 and was paid for by public donations. The figure sits in the posture of subduing Mara, legs crossed and the right hand reaching towards the earth. Its concrete structure is faced with small tiles of white Burmese marble, which is why it glows at sunrise and sunset.
A smaller golden-coloured Buddha sits beside it. Around the base, visitors write wishes on marble tiles and small brass bells that are hung on the trees.

Nakkerd Hill rises between Chalong and Kata, and the terrace looks in every direction. To the east you see Chalong Bay and the offshore islands. To the west, the beaches of Kata and Karon. On a very clear day you can make out more islands far out on the horizon.

The road up leaves the main route near Chalong and climbs for about six kilometres. Most visitors come by taxi, hired car or scooter. The road is steep and winding, so inexperienced riders should think twice. There is no regular public bus to the top.
Go early in the morning for cooler air and fewer tour groups, or about an hour before sunset. Remember that last entry is half an hour before closing.

tips: This is an active place of worship. Speak quietly and do not climb on the statue's base.
Monkeys live along the road. Do not feed them and keep bags closed.
Combine the visit with Wat Chalong, at the foot of the hill.
Bring water. There are a few stalls at the top but prices are higher.
faq: Is there an entrance fee?
No. Entry is free, and donations towards the upkeep of the site are welcome.
How long does a visit take?
About an hour at the top, plus the drive up and down.
What should I wear?
Cover your shoulders and knees. Sarongs are lent free at the entrance if you arrive in beachwear.
Can I walk up?
There are steep footpaths from the Kata and Karon side. They take an hour or more in full heat and are best attempted early in the morning with plenty of water.

stories.title: Phuket beaches, sorted by mood
stories.dek: One for families, one for quiet, one for doing nothing at all.
body: Phuket's west coast is one long run of bays, and each has its own character. From about May to October the sea is rougher. Swim only where there are lifeguards, and never when red flags are flying.

items.text: For families, and for beginner surfers in the wet season.
For a local feel.
For getting away from the road.
For miles of empty sand.
For crowds and nightlife.

p: From about November to April the Andaman Sea is calm and clear, and nearly every west-coast beach is safe for swimming. From May to October the south-west monsoon brings waves and strong rip currents. People drown on Phuket's beaches every year in these months.
Lifeguards mark safe areas with red-and-yellow flags. A red flag means do not enter the water at all. Take the flags seriously, even when the sea looks inviting.

The island is larger than it looks, about 50 kilometres from north to south, and the beaches are separated by steep headlands. The Phuket Smart Bus runs along the west coast between the airport and Rawai and is the cheapest way to move around. Taxis and ride-hailing cars are easy to find but cost far more than in Bangkok.
Many visitors rent scooters. The roads over the headlands are steep and accidents are common, so wear a helmet and check that your travel insurance covers riding.

Karon, next to Kata, is a long, wide beach with fine sand that squeaks underfoot. Surin and Bang Tao, further north, are quieter and lined with resorts. Nai Yang, near the airport, sits inside a national park and has a relaxed, local feel.

sections.h: A beach choice shaped by surf culture
p: The linked interview-led surf guide describes a growing community around Phuket’s beaches, with Kata and Bang Tao among the places where surf schools have established themselves. Its coverage is about surfing culture and seasonal waves, rather than a promise of calm water for every beach visit.

Use that distinction when choosing the kind of day you want: watching the surf, taking a locally supervised lesson or staying on shore. The article is background reading; check conditions with lifeguards and a qualified local operator on the day, and follow beach flags.

tips: Smoking is banned on many Thai beaches, including Patong, and fines are large.
Jellyfish appear at certain times of year. Lifeguard stations keep vinegar for stings.
Sunbeds are allowed only in marked zones. Bring a towel or mat.
The sun is strongest between 11am and 3pm. Use reef-safe sunscreen.
faq: Which beach is best for children?
Kata and Nai Harn, in the dry season, when the water is calm and the slope into the sea is gentle. Always swim near the lifeguards.
Can I walk from one beach to the next?
Kata and Karon are close enough to walk between in about twenty minutes. Most others are separated by steep headlands and need a vehicle.
When is the sea clearest?
From December to March, when there is little rain and almost no swell on the west coast.
Is there shade?
Nai Harn and Mai Khao have trees behind the sand. Elsewhere, bring an umbrella or rent one in the permitted zones.

stories.title: A morning in Phuket Old Town
stories.dek: Pastel shophouses, dim sum at dawn and coffee poured through a cloth filter.
body: Phuket Town was built on tin. The traders who grew rich from it, many of them Hokkien Chinese, left a few streets of Sino-Portuguese shophouses with tiled floors and arched walkways. Thalang Road, Dibuk Road and Soi Romanee are the best preserved.
Breakfast is the meal to come for. Start with small plates of dim sum, move on to yellow Hokkien noodles, and finish in a kopi shop.
On Sundays from 4pm to 10pm, Thalang Road closes to traffic for the Lard Yai walking street.

p: In the nineteenth century Phuket was one of the world's main sources of tin. The boom drew thousands of Hokkien Chinese workers and merchants, many of them by way of Penang in what is now Malaysia. They built the shophouses that give the old town its character: narrow fronts, long interiors with an open air well, and a covered walkway along the street to shelter pedestrians from sun and rain.

The style is usually called Sino-Portuguese. The community that grew up here, with its mix of Chinese and local customs, is known as Baba or Peranakan, and its food and dress are still part of daily life.

The Thai Hua Museum, in a handsome former Chinese-language school, tells the story of the tin trade and the families who ran it. The On On Hotel, opened in the late 1920s, was the island's first hotel and has been restored. Soi Romanee, once the red-light lane for miners, is now the prettiest street in town.
In 2015 UNESCO named Phuket a Creative City of Gastronomy, largely on the strength of the old town's cooking.

Local specialities are different from standard Thai restaurant food. Mee Hokkien is thick yellow noodles fried with pork and seafood. Moo hong is pork belly braised slowly with pepper and garlic. For something sweet, o-aew is a bowl of shaved ice with banana-seed jelly and red beans, found almost nowhere else in Thailand.

tips: Mornings are best. By noon it is too hot to enjoy walking.
Many cafes and small museums close on Mondays.
The Smart Bus does not serve the old town. Take a taxi, or one of the open-sided local buses that link the beaches with Phuket Town.
On Sundays, come at four for the walking street and stay for dinner.
faq: How long should I allow?
Half a day covers the main streets, a museum and a long breakfast. Add the evening if it is a Sunday.
Is it walkable?
Yes. The historic core is only a few blocks across, and the covered walkways give shade for much of the way.
What if it rains?
The arcades in front of the shophouses were designed for exactly that. You can walk most of Thalang Road under cover, and the museums and cafes are good places to wait out a shower.
Where does a taxi drop me?
Ask for Thalang Road. Parking in the old town is very limited, so arriving by taxi is easier than driving.

stories.title: Thadingyut 2026: the Festival of Lights is on 25 to 27 October
stories.dek: Three days of candles, lanterns and visits to elders mark the end of Buddhist Lent.
body: Thadingyut falls on the full moon of the seventh Burmese month. In 2026 the public holidays run from Sunday 25 to Tuesday 27 October, with the full-moon day on the 26th.

Homes and streets are strung with lights, and pagodas fill with candles after dark. Shwedagon and Sule are the places to see it in Yangon. It is also a time to pay respects to parents, teachers and older relatives.
A second festival of lights, Tazaungdaing, follows at the next full moon, on 23 and 24 November.

p: Thadingyut comes at the end of the three-month Buddhist rains retreat, a period when monks stay in their monasteries and lay people traditionally avoid weddings and moving house. Buddhists believe that on this full moon the Buddha returned to earth after spending the retreat teaching in a heavenly realm, and that his path was lit by rows of lamps.
People light their homes, streets and pagodas to welcome him back. It is the second most important festival of the year after the new-year water festival in April.

The festival is also a time for gadaw, the custom of paying respects to elders. Younger people visit parents, grandparents and teachers, bring gifts of food or cloth, and ask forgiveness for any wrongs of the past year. Offices and shops often hold their own ceremonies for senior staff.

The terraces of the Shwedagon Pagoda are lined with thousands of oil lamps and candles on the three evenings, and worshippers come in family groups. Downtown, the streets around Sule Pagoda are strung with coloured lights. Go at dusk, when the lamps are being lit, and stay for an hour or two.

tips: Government offices, banks and many businesses close for the three public holidays.
Dress modestly for pagoda visits and be ready to walk barefoot.
Buses and trains are crowded as people travel home. Book long-distance tickets early.
Check current travel advice for Myanmar before making plans.
faq: Can visitors join in?
Yes. Lighting a candle at a pagoda is welcomed. Behave as you would in any place of worship and follow what local families do.
What should I wear?
Clothes that cover shoulders and knees. You will walk barefoot on pagoda grounds, so sandals that slip off are practical.
Are shops open?
Many family-run shops close for the holidays. Hotels, larger restaurants and some markets stay open.
How is it different from Tazaungdaing?
Tazaungdaing falls one lunar month later and marks the end of the rainy season. It is known for overnight robe-weaving contests at pagodas and, in Shan State, a hot-air balloon festival.

stories.title: Shwedagon at dusk: a first-timer's guide
stories.dek: When to go, what to wear and how to find your birthday corner.
body: The Shwedagon Pagoda is a 99-metre gilded stupa on Singuttara Hill, and the most sacred Buddhist site in Myanmar. It is visible from most of the city.
Arrive an hour before sunset. Shoes and socks come off at the foot of the stairs, and shoulders and knees must be covered. Walk clockwise around the terrace.

Around the base are eight planetary posts, one for each day of the week, with Wednesday split in two. Find the one for the day you were born and pour water over the Buddha image there, as local visitors do. Foreign visitors pay an entrance fee. We could not confirm the current amount, so check at the gate.

p: Tradition says the Shwedagon is more than 2,500 years old and holds eight hairs of the Buddha, brought to this hill by two merchant brothers. Historians and archaeologists think the first stupa was built by the Mon people some time between the sixth and tenth centuries.

It has been rebuilt and raised many times. In the fifteenth century Queen Shinsawbu gave her own weight in gold to gild it, beginning a tradition that continues today. The stupa reached its present height of about 99 metres after repairs in the eighteenth century. The jewelled umbrella at the very top was donated by King Mindon in 1871 and is set with thousands of diamonds and other gems.

Four covered stairways climb the hill from the north, south, east and west. The southern entrance, guarded by a pair of giant lion figures, is the most used. Several entrances also have lifts or escalators.

At the top, a wide marble terrace surrounds the main stupa, crowded with smaller shrines, pavilions and bells. Custom is to walk around it clockwise. The marble gets very hot under the midday sun, which is one more reason to come early or late.

As the sun goes down, the gold changes from yellow to deep orange, and then floodlights come on. Families arrive after work to pray, light candles and sit together on the terrace. It feels less like a monument and more like a town square.

tips: Shoes and socks are not allowed anywhere on the hill. Bring a bag to carry them.
Wear trousers or a skirt below the knee and cover your shoulders. Longyis can be borrowed at the entrance.
Bring a wet wipe for your feet afterwards.
Keep your ticket sticker visible. Staff check it on the terrace.
faq: How long should I spend there?
An hour and a half to two hours, timed so that you are on the terrace as the sun sets.
Is there an entrance fee?
Yes, for foreign visitors. You pay at a booth at the entrance and receive a sticker to wear.
Can I take photographs?
Yes, on the terrace. Be considerate of people who are praying, and do not pose with your back to a Buddha image.
Is a guide worth it?
Licensed guides wait near the entrances and can explain the shrines, the planetary posts and the history. Agree a price before you start.

stories.title: Three hours on the Yangon Circular Railway
stories.dek: A 45.9 km commuter loop that doubles as the best cheap tour of the city.
body: The Circular Railway opened in 1954 and loops through 39 stations from Yangon Central. A full circuit takes about three hours.
You do not need to ride all of it. Many visitors go as far as Danyingon, where a produce market spills across the platform, and return the same way.
Our most recent source for timetables and fares dates from 2024. Confirm both at Yangon Central before you set out.

p: This is a working commuter line, not a tourist train. Carriages have bench seats along the sides, windows that open and vendors who walk the aisle selling fruit, boiled eggs and betel. People board with sacks of vegetables, live chickens and bicycles.
The train rarely moves faster than a bicycle, so you have time to watch the city thin out into market gardens and villages and then gather itself again.

Yangon Central Station, where most visitors start, was rebuilt in 1954 with tiered roofs in traditional Burmese style. Insein, in the north-west, is a busy junction. Danyingon, at the top of the loop, is the highlight: a wholesale produce market spreads across the platforms and the tracks, and the train noses through it at walking pace.

Three hours on a hard bench is a long time. A common plan is to ride from Yangon Central to Danyingon, get off to look around the market, and take a train or taxi back. Trains run in both directions, so ask at the ticket window which one is leaving next.

tips: Bring water, a hat and small change for snacks.
Sit on the shaded side. It changes as the train turns.
Older carriages have no air conditioning and basic toilets.
Timetables change. Confirm departure times at the station on the day.
faq: Where do I buy a ticket?
At the ticket office on the platform at Yangon Central Station, shortly before departure. Carry your passport, as it has sometimes been asked for.
What is the best time to ride?
A morning departure. The market at Danyingon is busiest early, and the carriages are cooler.
Are there toilets and food on board?
Toilets are basic. Vendors sell fruit, snacks and drinks in the aisle, but bring your own water.
Is it safe?
Ride in daylight, keep your belongings close and read current travel advice for Myanmar before you go.

stories.title: How to order in a Yangon tea shop
stories.dek: Low stools, sweet milk tea and the national breakfast.
body: The tea shop is Yangon's living room. People come for a cup of strong tea with condensed milk and stay for the news, the football and a second breakfast.

Order your tea by sweetness and strength, then look at what is coming out of the kitchen. Mohinga, a fish and rice-noodle soup, is the national breakfast and is often finished by nine. Fried dough sticks are for dunking. A pot of plain green tea on the table is free.
The shops we list were last confirmed by sources from 2020 to 2024. Check that they are open before you make a special trip.

p: Burmese tea is black, brewed strong and mixed with condensed and evaporated milk. You order by how sweet and how strong you want it. Asking for the regular blend gets a balanced cup. There are names for sweeter, milkier versions and for stronger, more bitter ones, and regulars are particular about theirs.
A flask of plain Chinese tea sits on every table and is free. People drink it between sips of the sweet tea and to rinse their cups.

Tea shops are where people eat breakfast and afternoon snacks. Besides mohinga, look for samosas, steamed buns, flaky flatbread served with boiled peas, and a salad of thick rice noodles dressed with chicken curry and chickpea flour.

The most famous Burmese dish of all is also built on tea: laphet thoke, a salad of pickled tea leaves with fried beans, peanuts, sesame and garlic. It is sharp, crunchy and slightly bitter, and it is offered to guests in every home.

Sit wherever there is space. Snacks are often placed on the table without being ordered, and you pay only for what you eat. To call a waiter, customers traditionally make a short kissing sound, which is not rude here. Tea shops open before dawn and many are busiest between six and nine in the morning.

For a related food story, The linked Singapore dining feature profiled Club Rangoon in Duxton, Singapore. The article describes co-founder Nelson Htoo’s family recipes and a restaurant design inspired by Burmese teahouses, where eating and conversation share the same space.

This is a useful cultural connection for readers interested in Yangon’s food traditions, but Club Rangoon is in Singapore. It is not a Yangon venue recommendation or an update on local conditions. Read the original for that restaurant’s story; use our Yangon guide’s separate travel advisory when considering a visit to Myanmar.
sections.sourceNote: Related coverage from Singapore; this source does not describe a venue in Yangon.

tips: Go early. Mohinga is a breakfast dish and the pot is often empty by nine.
Carry small kyat notes. Tea shops do not take cards.
Street-side shops use low plastic stools. Indoor ones have proper tables.
If you have a delicate stomach, choose hot, freshly cooked items over salads.
faq: Are tea shops welcoming to solo travellers and women?
Yes. Early-morning street shops are mostly full of men on their way to work, but families and groups of friends use them all day and nobody minds a visitor.
Is there vegetarian food?
Potato samosas, boiled peas with flatbread and several noodle salads are meat-free. Ask for tea leaf salad without dried shrimp.
What are the opening hours?
Most open before dawn and close in the early evening. A few city-centre shops stay open late.
How do I know what I owe?
Staff count the plates and cups on your table when you ask to pay. Snacks you did not touch are taken back and not charged.

stories.title: Downtown Yangon on foot
stories.dek: From Sule Pagoda to the river through a grid of grand old buildings.
body: Downtown Yangon was laid out as a grid in the 1850s, with Sule Pagoda at its centre. That makes it hard to get lost and easy to wander.
Begin at Sule and walk east and south along Pansodan Street. Look up as you go: the upper floors are a catalogue of a century of architecture, some restored and some held together by tree roots.
Finish on Strand Road by the river. Bogyoke Aung San Market, a few blocks north-west of Sule, is closed on Mondays.

p: Sule Pagoda sits in a roundabout that the city's planners made the centre of their grid. Beside it are City Hall, completed in 1936 with Burmese-style tiered roofs on a colonial frame, and the park that holds the Independence Monument. Across the park stands the red-brick High Court with its clock tower, finished in 1911.

Pansodan Street runs south from here towards the river and was the business address of colonial Rangoon. Its banks, shipping offices and trading houses are still standing, some restored and some in gentle decay. Pavement booksellers spread second-hand books along the lower end.

On Strand Road, facing the water, are the Strand Hotel of 1901 and the old customs and port buildings. A few blocks east is the Secretariat, the vast former seat of government where the independence leader Aung San was assassinated in 1947.

Downtown Yangon has one of the largest collections of colonial-era buildings in Southeast Asia. Decades of isolation meant there was little money to knock them down. A local conservation group, the Yangon Heritage Trust, has put blue plaques on many of the most important ones, and reading them as you go turns the walk into a history lesson.

Start by 7.30am, when the streets are cool and the tea shops are full. Pavements are broken in places and often blocked by stalls, so you will spend some of the time walking in the road. Watch for open drains.

tips: The whole route is about three kilometres and takes two hours with stops.
Carry water and wear a hat. Shade is limited after 10am.
Ask before photographing people, monks and anything official.
Check current travel advice for Myanmar before making plans.
faq: Is downtown easy to navigate?
Yes. The streets form a grid, and the narrow north-south ones are numbered. Sule Pagoda is visible from many corners and makes a reliable landmark.
Can I go inside the old buildings?
Some. The Strand Hotel's lobby and cafe are open to visitors, and the General Post Office is a working building. Others are offices or are closed for restoration.
Where can I stop for a break?
Pavement tea shops are on almost every block. For air conditioning, the cafe at the Strand is the traditional choice.
Is it safe to walk?
Go in daylight, watch your footing on broken pavements and read current travel advice for Myanmar before you travel.

stories.title: Deepavali is on 8 November, with a Monday holiday
stories.dek: Little India lights up for the Hindu festival of lights.
body: Deepavali falls on Sunday 8 November 2026. Because it lands on a Sunday, Monday 9 November is a public holiday as well, according to the Ministry of Manpower.
Serangoon Road in Little India is decorated with light arches for several weeks before the day, and a festive bazaar sets up in the side streets.

p: Deepavali, also written Diwali, is the Hindu festival of lights. It marks the victory of light over darkness and of good over evil. Families clean and decorate their homes, light rows of small oil lamps, wear new clothes and visit relatives with boxes of sweets.
In Singapore it is one of the major public holidays and is celebrated well beyond the Hindu community.

Little India is the centre. Arches of coloured lights span Serangoon Road for weeks beforehand, and the side streets fill with a festive bazaar selling garlands, lamps, saris, henna painting and snacks. The Sri Veeramakaliamman Temple on Serangoon Road is busy with worshippers throughout.
Doorways are decorated with patterns drawn in coloured rice powder. They are made fresh and are meant to be admired, so step around them.

Take the MRT to Little India or Farrer Park. The streets are at their liveliest in the evenings of the final week and are very crowded on the night before the holiday. Go on a weekday evening if you want room to walk.

tips: Many shops in Little India close on the holiday itself. Visit in the days before.
Shoes come off at temple doors, and shoulders and knees should be covered.
Try murukku, a crunchy spiral snack, and the milk-based sweets sold by weight.
Carry cash for bazaar stalls.
faq: Is Deepavali the same as Diwali?
Yes. Deepavali is the name used in Tamil and across Singapore and Malaysia. Diwali is the form more common in northern India.
Are shops and attractions open on the holiday?
Shopping centres and major attractions are generally open. Government offices are closed, and many family businesses in Little India take the day off.
Can visitors enter the temples?
Yes, respectfully. Remove your shoes, dress modestly and avoid walking in front of people who are praying. Ask before photographing anyone.
How long do the street lights stay up?
The light-up runs for several weeks before the day and usually continues for a short time afterwards.
What should I eat?
Little India's restaurants serve vegetarian meals on banana leaves, biryani and a wide range of sweets. Snack stalls at the bazaar sell fried savouries by the bag.

stories.title: One hungry day, two hawker centres
stories.dek: A lunch, a supper and a plan for the queues.
body: Hawker centres are how Singapore eats, and in 2020 UNESCO added hawker culture to its list of intangible heritage. The rules are simple: find a table first, mark it with a packet of tissues, then join the longest line you can stand.
Go to Maxwell Food Centre in Chinatown late in the morning for chicken rice, before the office crowd arrives.
After dark, head to Lau Pa Sat. The street beside its cast-iron hall closes to traffic and fills with satay grills.

p: Until the 1960s, cooked food in Singapore was sold from carts and pavement stalls. The government moved the hawkers into purpose-built open-air centres with running water and drains, and rents were kept low so that prices could stay low too. More than a hundred centres now operate across the island, and most people eat at one several times a week.

Each stall specialises in one dish. Beyond chicken rice, look for char kway teow, flat rice noodles fried over fierce heat with egg and cockles. Laksa is noodles in a spiced coconut broth. Carrot cake contains no carrot at all: it is cubes of steamed radish cake fried with egg.
Breakfast is kaya toast, spread with coconut jam and a slab of cold butter, with two soft-boiled eggs and a cup of local coffee.

Local coffee has its own vocabulary. Kopi comes with condensed milk. Kopi-O is black with sugar. Kopi-C uses evaporated milk. Add kosong for no sugar and peng for iced. The same words work for tea, which is teh.

Lau Pa Sat means old market. Its octagonal cast-iron frame was made in Glasgow and assembled here in 1894, and the building is a national monument. Come in the evening, when Boon Tat Street beside it closes to cars and the satay sellers set up their grills.

The linked city guide highlights Old Airport Road Food Centre as another place to explore Singapore’s hawker cooking. The centre dates to 1973; the article notes seating and cooling improvements made in 2024. It also points readers towards dishes such as fried kway teow and prawn noodles.

If your stay is longer than one day, our suggestion is to make this a separate food outing rather than squeezing a third centre into the route above. Individual stalls keep their own schedules, so check the ones you want before setting off.

tips: Return your tray and crockery to the racks. It is required by law.
A packet of tissues on a table means it is taken.
Many stalls close one or two days a week, and some sell out by early afternoon.
Most stalls take cash and local QR payments. Cards are rarely accepted.
faq: Is hawker food hygienic?
Stalls are licensed and regularly inspected. Food is cooked to order in open view, and standards are high.
Are there halal and vegetarian options?
Yes. Halal stalls display their certification, and most centres have at least one Indian vegetarian stall.
When are hawker centres busiest?
From noon to 1.30pm and from 6.30pm to 8pm. Go a little before or after to find a table easily.
How much does a meal cost?
A plate at a hawker stall costs a fraction of a restaurant main course, which is why locals of every income eat there.

stories.title: Tokyo listening bars for beginners
stories.dek: Where the record is the point and talking is optional.
body: A listening bar is built around its sound system. The owner chooses the records, you choose a drink, and for the length of an album side nobody says much. The tradition grew out of the jazz cafes of the 1950s, when imported records cost more than most people could afford.
House rules vary. Some bars ask for silence, others just for low voices. If in doubt, watch the regulars. Many add a small cover charge and expect you to keep ordering.

p: Japan's jazz cafes, called jazz kissa, date back to the late 1920s and had their golden age in the 1950s and 1960s. Imported records were far too expensive for most people to own, so fans paid for a cup of coffee and listened to the owner's collection on the best equipment in town.
Many of those cafes survive. Alongside them, a younger generation has opened listening bars that play soul, ambient, city pop and electronic music with the same seriousness.

Rooms are small, often with fewer than twenty seats, and the speakers are usually the largest objects in them. The owner chooses each record with care and may display the sleeve on the counter while it plays.
Most places add a cover charge to the bill, sometimes with a small snack. One drink per hour or so is the accepted pace. Whisky highballs and coffee are the standard orders.

Shinjuku, Shibuya and Shimokitazawa have the highest concentration, and the western suburbs along the Chuo line are known for long-established jazz cafes. Many are on upper floors or in basements with only a small sign at street level.

The linked listening-bar feature traces Tokyo’s listening bars to the postwar jazz-kissaten tradition and distinguishes recorded-music spaces from live-performance venues. Its examples include Jazz Inn Uncle Tom in Sangenjaya and Spincoaster near Yoyogi, illustrating how coffee shops and evening bars can both put the music at the centre of a visit.
